summary: Lays out an architecture and plan for handing out IP addresses so that they can be aggregated, helping steer the Internet toward its address assignment and aggregation strategy. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: If you give out street numbers in tidy blocks, mail sorters need fewer signs. This memo describes how to give out Internet addresses in tidy blocks.

subtitle: The architecture that made Internet routing scalable through hierarchical address allocation

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew, flat routing tables where every domain knew every other domain's network numbers became unscalable. Address assignments based on administrative boundaries rather than network topology prevented aggregation.
tldr.mechanism: CIDR allocates addresses hierarchically so that topologically connected networks hold prefixes derived from their provider's prefix, enabling routing information to be summarized at domain boundaries instead of listing individual networks.
tldr.outcome: This architecture became foundational to Internet growth; it enabled the sustained scaling of inter-domain routing for decades. It is now Historic as routing evolved, but its principles remain embedded in how the Internet works.

today: RFC 1518 is Historic. Its architecture became the foundation of Internet scaling and remains embedded in today's addressing practices through CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing). The hierarchical allocation model it describes has been successful for decades, though IPv6 deployment and changes in Internet topology have introduced new considerations not covered in this document.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content: This document provides an architecture and plan for allocating IP addresses in the Internet, intended to guide the Internet toward an address assignment and aggregating strategy. IP address space is a scarce shared resource that must be managed for the community's benefit. The technical challenge is twofold: the Internet has many routing domains under different administrative authorities, and the managers of those domains need both administrative independence and global routing scalability. This RFC focuses on the technical aspects of address allocation, particularly how to assign addresses to support hierarchical routing data abstraction through which reachability information can be summarized.
sections.eli5: The Internet is divided into many networks run by different organizations. Each network needs its own addresses, but if you assign them randomly, routers must track each one individually, which does not scale.

sections.title: Why Address Allocation Matters for Routing
sections.content: IP routing is divided into three parts: between end systems and routers, between routers in the same domain (interior routing), and between domains (exterior routing). The fundamental insight is that reachability information can be abstracted: if all addresses within a routing domain are drawn from a single IP prefix, then boundary routers can summarize the entire domain as one prefix instead of listing every network number. If addresses are scattered among many unrelated prefixes, no summarization is possible and boundary information must be an enumerated list of every network. In a small Internet, flat routing works; in a growing Internet with tens of thousands of domains, flat routing becomes intractable. Hierarchical address allocation enables hierarchical routing data abstraction.
sections.eli5: Think of mail delivery. If everyone in a town has an address based on their street, mail carriers can say 'Main Street goes this way' without tracking each house. If houses have random addresses, you need a separate route for each.

sections.title: Hierarchical Address Allocation Structure
sections.content:
The recommended structure is hierarchical: continental authorities allocate address space to national or regional providers, which allocate to direct service providers (such as regional networks), which allocate to sites (leaf routing domains). A backbone provider might be allocated a prefix such as 198.0.0.0/8, allocate /16 prefixes to regional providers, which in turn allocate /24 or /25 prefixes to sites. Each site addresses its internal networks from its allocated prefix. This structure means that when a site's address is based on its provider's prefix, all of the site's networks can be summarized with a single prefix at the backbone level. As the Internet grows, additional levels of hierarchy can be inserted without breaking existing addresses.

At each level, the provider advertises its own prefix to higher levels, allowing multi-level aggregation. For example, a backbone needs only to advertise continental prefixes to other backbones, while within a continent it advertises provider prefixes, and providers advertise site prefixes locally.
sections.eli5: Addresses flow from top to bottom. The backbone gives big blocks to providers, providers give smaller blocks to cities or companies, and cities or companies give small blocks to departments. Each level can summarize its children with one prefix.

sections.title: Multi-homed and Special Cases
sections.content: Sites connected to multiple providers (multi-homed sites) present a challenge: if each provider gives the site a separate prefix, then each provider must tell the backbone about that site separately, creating extra routing table entries. The document describes four solutions: the site obtains one global address prefix and each provider tells the backbone about it (requiring many backbone entries worldwide); the site uses provider-specific prefixes for each connection and announces each separately (requiring more work at the site and providers); the site uses a default primary prefix but announces alternatives selectively to specific providers for backup; or multiple providers sharing customers form address pools for different combinations of attached customers. Each approach trades off different costs: routing table size, administrative complexity, backup route availability, and policy routing ability. Private links between organizations pose less difficulty since their routing information is not exchanged globally. Zero-homed organizations (those with no public Internet connection) must still use globally unique addresses on private links to avoid conflicts if future connections are made.
sections.eli5: A company connected to two providers is tricky: does it use one address block or two? Using one means the backbone sees it in many places. Using two means the company must manage two separate addresses.

sections.title: Transition and Continental Aggregation
sections.content: As the Internet topology evolves, organizations may change providers and need to renumber. The document recommends that renumbering happen gradually: the old address remains advertised while the new address is brought up, and gradually traffic transitions. For large address changes, longest-match routing ensures packets destined for old addresses still reach the destination through intermediate providers until routing tables update. Continental aggregation forms an additional hierarchy level, where all addresses within a continent are drawn from a continental prefix, allowing inter-continental routing to operate on just a few prefixes. Exceptions for multi-continental providers can be handled similarly to multi-homed domains. The document notes that policy routing considerations favor allocating addresses so that organizations with similar policies can be aggregated together.
sections.eli5: When a company moves to a new provider and gets a new address, the old address still works temporarily while routing tables update. By continent, all of Europe might use addresses starting with 194, all of North America with 198, so routers need only a few rules for intercontinental traffic.
